title: Delhi's air is the worst in 288 days, with 'severe' levels forecast before Diwali
dek: The capital's average air quality index reached 377 on Wednesday, and 22 of its 59 monitoring stations were in the 'severe' band. Forecasters expect conditions to worsen on Friday and Saturday.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Delhi's air quality on Wednesday, 4 November, was the worst it has been in 288 days. The city's 24-hour average air quality index (AQI) in the Central Pollution Control Board's 4 pm bulletin was 377, in the "very poor" band and close to the "severe" threshold of 401, one report said. It was the highest reading since 20 January, when the index stood at 378.

Of Delhi's 59 monitoring stations, 22 recorded "severe" air, 32 "very poor" and five "poor". The highest readings were at IIT Delhi (458), Jahangirpuri and Punjabi Bagh (448 each) and Mundka (439). The forecast for the next few days, cited in the same report, is "very poor" air on Thursday and "severe" air on Friday and Saturday, the eve of Diwali on 8 November.

## What the numbers mean

The AQI combines the levels of several pollutants into one number. On the Central Pollution Control Board's scale, 0-50 is "good", 101-200 "moderate", 201-300 "poor", 301-400 "very poor" and 401-500 "severe". The board describes "very poor" air as likely to cause breathing illness on long exposure, and "severe" air as affecting healthy people and seriously affecting those with lung and heart disease.

On Wednesday the main pollutant was PM10, coarser dust-sized particles, after three days in which the finer PM2.5 particles, which reach deeper into the lungs, had dominated.

## Where the pollution comes from

The government's Decision Support System, run by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology in Pune, estimates where Delhi's pollution comes from each day. For Wednesday, it put the share from crop-residue burning in neighbouring states at 20.2%, and from vehicles in Delhi at 15.5%. Smaller shares came from homes (3.8%), industry (2.9%), construction (2.2%), waste burning (1.3%) and road dust (1.1%). Nearby districts of the National Capital Region also contributed, led by Ghaziabad at 7%.

Satellites detected 467 farm fires across six states on Wednesday, according to the CREAMS laboratory at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute: 157 in Madhya Pradesh, 151 in Punjab, 111 in Rajasthan, 33 in Uttar Pradesh, 10 in Haryana and 5 in Uttarakhand. From 15 September to 4 November, it counted about 4,800 burning incidents in seven states and Union Territories.

Weather also matters. In early November, colder nights and light winds trap pollutants close to the ground. On Wednesday the minimum temperature at Safdarjung was 16.1°C, and the maximum 29.8°C.

## What is being done

The Commission for Air Quality Management imposed Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) across Delhi and the NCR on Monday, 2 November. One report said that the measures include mechanical road sweeping, water sprinkling, anti-smog guns and higher parking fees to discourage private cars, and that by Tuesday Delhi Police had checked 7,657 vehicles at the city's borders since Sunday and turned back 609 that did not meet the rules. Stage III, with tighter curbs on construction and older vehicles, is normally triggered when the AQI is expected to cross 401.

## What happens next

Firecrackers are the main worry for the coming days. On Tuesday the Supreme Court asked the Centre to look into reports that all kinds of firecrackers, licensed or not, were being sold openly in Delhi despite the conditions it had set for Diwali. The Central Pollution Control Board publishes its bulletin every day at 4 pm.
